solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Function of aide in prisoner release (6)

blocks.note: a PA is a personal assistant
role = function; 'function of aide' is the aide's role, so the aide comes first

annotation.surface: A job description: what an assistant does while a convict is let out.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an office helper, but the word order inside 'function of aide' is a possessive that the answer reads in reverse.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the conditional early freeing of an inmate on good behaviour, with a promise to keep the terms.

entries.clue: Advertise vacancy where result’s already decided? (3-2,3)

annotation.definitionNote: the second definition describes the thing rather than naming it: a situation where the outcome is fixed

blocks.note: read literally: post (display) a position on a notice board
a fraud or stitch-up arranged in advance

annotation.surface: A cynic's view of a recruitment advert when the post has already been promised to an insider.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses meet: a job advertised when the winner is already chosen is a put-up job in both ways at once.
annotation.definitionFit: Literally, to put up a job is to advertise it; idiomatically, a put-up job is a rigged scheme whose outcome was settled beforehand.

entries.clue: Crop warped in the ear (3)

indicatorNotes.in the ear: what reaches the ear is a sound, not a spelling, so the word is judged by how it is heard

annotation.surface: A farmer's complaint that the grain has come up bent in the ear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the ear' pretends to be the ear of a cereal plant, which fits the crop; it is the sound instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a cereal grass grown in fields for grain, whisky and bread.

entries.clue: Lower rent supported by county (3,4)

indicatorNotes.supported by: a thing supported by another rests on top of it, so in a down clue the first piece sits above the second

blocks.note: one of the six counties of Northern Ireland

annotation.surface: A landlord's rent propped up by the local council.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lower rent' reads as a cheaper tenancy, but 'Lower' is a verb standing alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to lower a rope or a blind is to release it gradually downwards.

entries.clue: Does the author have what it takes to keep clubs friendly? (8)

indicatorNotes.keep: to keep something is to hold it, so the outer word holds the club inside it

blocks.note: the author = I, the setter, so 'does the author' becomes 'am I'

annotation.surface: A writer wondering whether they have the tact to keep a golf club on good terms.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter answers his own question, 'Am I able?', with the card suit slipped into the middle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: agreeable and free of conflict, as a settlement between parties can be.

entries.clue: Grammar essentially a barrier, monarch for one abandoned Japanese (5,9)

indicatorNotes.essentially: the essence of a word is its core, so take the central letter
indicatorNotes.for one: the monarch is offered as one example of the category the answer wants

blocks.note: the monarch is an orange and black species of this insect

annotation.surface: A cryptic list of school grammar, a barricade and a king, ending with someone left behind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Monarch' wants to be a king; it is the insect. The heroine of Puccini's opera is Cio-Cio-San, left behind by her American husband Pinkerton.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the title character of Puccini's opera is a young Japanese bride deserted by her American naval husband.

entries.clue: City’s vital energy keeping queen up (7)

indicatorNotes.keeping: to keep something is to hold it, so the energy word holds the queen inside it
indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, a word sent up reads from the bottom, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: chi (qi) is the life force in Chinese thought
Queen Anne, the last Stuart monarch

annotation.surface: A city's life force holding up its queen.
annotation.walkthrough: The queen is sent up the column before the life force closes around her.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the capital of Tamil Nadu in south-east India, formerly called Madras.

entries.clue: The Black Horse loans out a room you’d look better to leave (6,5)

annotation.definition: a room you’d look better to leave

indicatorNotes.out: letters put out of place come back in a new order

blocks.note: Anna Sewell's novel is about a horse called Black Beauty, so the horse surnamed Black is Beauty

annotation.surface: A pub called The Black Horse lending out a function room.
annotation.walkthrough: The Black Horse reads as a pub sign, and a pub has rooms for hire; the horse is the one from the children's classic. The definition is cryptic: you come out looking better.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a place for hairdressing and treatments, which you leave looking better than when you walked in.

entries.clue: No longer cheeking master? (6)

annotation.surface: A pupil who has stopped giving lip to the schoolmaster.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Master' looks like a teacher being cheeked; it is the definition, someone who has mastered a craft.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a master of chess or carpentry is a person with complete skill in it.

entries.clue: Dismissal from Wellington’s command? (5,2,3,4)

blocks.note: a wellington is a rubber boot, so its command is an instruction issued by footwear

annotation.surface: A general being sacked by the Duke of Wellington.
annotation.walkthrough: Wellington looks like the Duke giving orders; it is the rubber boot named after him, and the question mark flags the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: getting the order of the boot means being kicked out; read literally, it is a command from a boot.

entries.clue: Better grind out a result here? (5,6)

indicatorNotes.out: to grind something out is to work it into shape, so the letters are reworked into a new order

annotation.surface: A coach urging his team to battle for a win at this ground.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is the Test cricket ground in Nottingham, where a side might well grind out a result; the whole clue reads as the definition too.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a cricket ground, a place where matches are fought out to a result.

entries.clue: One within range for each record (3)

blocks.note: a = per, as in five pounds a head
an LP is a long-playing record

annotation.surface: A price list: so much for each record in the range.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Range' looks like a product line; it is a mountain range.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a single high mountain, one peak in a chain.

entries.clue: Receiving bill, face down innkeeper (7)

indicatorNotes.Receiving: a word receiving something takes it in, so the outer word holds the bill inside

blocks.note: a bill is a poster, an ad

annotation.surface: A landlord handed the bill and sprawled face down on the floor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill' suggests the tab at the inn; it is an advertising bill.
annotation.definitionFit: A foreign-language synonym: the Italian word for the landlord or proprietor of an inn.

entries.clue: Official initially dropped, only had a most unreliable Welsh linesman (5,6)

indicatorNotes.initially: at the start, so it takes the first letter of official
indicatorNotes.dropped: something dropped is let go, so that letter leaves the fodder
indicatorNotes.most unreliable: letters that are unreliable cannot be trusted to stay in their given order

blocks.note: first letter of Official, to be removed
ONLYHADAMOST with its first O removed, the anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A football grumble: the referee's assistant from Wales was the least reliable official.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Linesman' looks like a football official; here it is a man of lines, a poet. The answer wrote Under Milk Wood.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the most famous Welsh poet of the twentieth century, a writer of lines.

entries.clue: Mass this month either side of Easter in church (7)

indicatorNotes.either side of: the two sides of a word are its edges, so take the letters at each end of Easter

blocks.note: inst. (instant) = of this month, in old business letters

annotation.surface: A church notice about Mass being said around Easter this month.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mass' belongs in the church scene but is only the physics symbol.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by type: a large or important church, originally one attached to a monastery, as at York.

entries.clue: Poem roughly about area belonging to university city (7,7)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the phrase for roughly goes around the rest

annotation.surface: A rough description of a poem set around a university town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' looks like an anagram signal, but it is a two-word phrase split to wrap everything else. The poem is Ariosto's Italian epic.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Ariosto's sixteenth-century Italian epic about the madness of the knight Roland.

entries.clue: One beaten by a different sort of player in a frame of snooker (8)

annotation.definition: One beaten by a different sort of player

blocks.clueFragment: One beaten by a different sort of player
blocks.note: a percussion instrument struck by an orchestral musician rather than a sportsman
the wooden frame used to rack the red balls

annotation.surface: A snooker player losing a frame to an opponent with an unusual style.
annotation.walkthrough: A frame of snooker is normally one game; here it is the literal frame that sets the reds, and the 'different sort of player' is a musician.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a three-sided steel percussion instrument struck with a beater, and the three-sided frame that racks snooker balls.

entries.clue: Booted, finally get them sparkling, in military order (7,7)

indicatorNotes.Booted: booted about means kicked around, so the letters are scattered
indicatorNotes.finally: at the end, so it takes the last letter of get

annotation.surface: A sergeant ordering recruits to polish their boots until they shine for parade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Booted' sits among boots and shine as footwear; it is the anagram instruction, as in booted about. The answer is the medieval crusading order.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a medieval order of warrior monks founded to protect pilgrims to Jerusalem.

entries.clue: Gear raised a very large stone (7)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, a word raised reads from the bottom up, so its letters run backwards

annotation.surface: A crane lifting a huge boulder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very large' reads as one idea; it splits into two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by type: a fire opal, a gemstone whose light seems to move as it turns.

entries.clue: A parent myself, backing your ostentatious ceremony (7)

indicatorNotes.backing: to back is to move backwards, so the abbreviation for your runs in reverse

annotation.surface: A parent announcing support for your showy celebration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like support for the ceremony; it is a direction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: showy, pretentious ritual, from the masked mummers' plays.

entries.clue: Chafe over endlessly prolific set of instructions (6)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, a piece over another sits above it
indicatorNotes.endlessly: without its end, so the last letter of rich goes

blocks.note: RICH (prolific, fertile) without its last letter

annotation.surface: Complaining about a manual that goes on and on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly prolific' reads as never-ending output; it is a trimming instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the directions printed at the head of an exam paper or service book.

entries.clue: Take off tights, possibly grabbing pair at the back, and throw (7)

indicatorNotes.grabbing: to grab something is to take hold of it, so the invented word takes the letter inside it
indicatorNotes.at the back: the back of a word is its end, so take the last letter of pair

blocks.note: an invented verb: to remove hose (tights); 'possibly' flags the coinage

annotation.surface: Someone struggling out of their tights, grabbing at the back, then flinging them away.
annotation.walkthrough: Hose are tights, so the made-up verb for taking them off is fair once 'possibly' admits it is not a real word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to throw a rider from the saddle.

entries.clue: Citizen breaks into a run around country (7)

indicatorNotes.breaks into: a burglar who breaks into a house ends up inside it, so the citizen goes inside
indicatorNotes.around: turned around means facing the other way, so A and R swap order

annotation.surface: A citizen breaking into a jog around the country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Citizen' is left vague on purpose: any nationality could fit, and only the letters around it pin it to the Gulf state.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a country in south-eastern Europe on the Black Sea.

entries.clue: A little spirit, dismissing opening batter with it (3)

indicatorNotes.dismissing opening: to dismiss is to send away, so the opening letter is sent away

blocks.note: a dram is a small measure of whisky; its first letter D goes

annotation.surface: A cricketer taking a nip of whisky after the opening batter is out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dismissing opening batter' reads as cricket; the dismissal is of a letter, and the definition is 'batter with it'.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the heavy beam or battering tool you batter a gate with.

entries.clue: Bearing up, in case police finally call (11)

indicatorNotes.finally: at the end, so it takes the last letter of police

blocks.note: 'should it rain' = in case it rains
to ring = to call on the phone

annotation.surface: Coping bravely, just in case the police ring.
annotation.walkthrough: The conditional 'in case' is the hard piece: 'should you need help' means in case you need help.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: taking a burden up onto your shoulders and carrying it.

entries.clue: Sort of mishap, map in parts missing (3)

indicatorNotes.in parts missing: missing in parts means lost piece by piece, so the letters go from different places

blocks.note: its three letters are removed separately from the longer word

annotation.surface: An explorer's minor accident: the map has come apart.
annotation.walkthrough: MAP is not a run of letters in MISHAP: its M, A and P come out from different places, which is what 'in parts' allows.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: used on its own, the suffix means more or less, roughly.

entries.clue: Randomly choose from Spooner’s few remaining beds (4,4)

indicatorNotes.Spooner’s: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so swap them here

blocks.note: last = the final few remaining; it takes the C sound from the second word
cots = beds; it takes the L sound from the first word

annotation.surface: A hotelier picking at random from the last few beds available.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Few remaining' is the stretch: the last ones are the few left.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to decide by drawing marked tokens, leaving the choice to chance.

entries.clue: Fruit hard to find in foreign school (6)

indicatorNotes.to find in: something found in a place is inside it, so the hard letter goes inside the school

blocks.note: a lycée is a French secondary school

annotation.surface: A child hunting for an exotic fruit in a school abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foreign' tells you the school is not English: it is the French word for a secondary school.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a small Chinese fruit with a rough red skin and white flesh.
